entities.name: PMID:25074374
observations: Fukuoka, Western Japan: time-stratified case-crossover study of 3,068 AMI hospitalizations from April 2003 to December 2010.
Asian dust events 0–4 days before admission were significantly associated with AMI incidence; the association was particularly significant 4 days before admission.
Adjusted for ambient temperature and relative humidity.

entities.name: PMID:29020374
observations: Kumamoto, Japan: time-stratified case-crossover study of 3,713 AMI patients from April 2010 to March 2015.
Asian dust one day before onset was associated with AMI (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.09–1.95), especially non-ST-elevation MI (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.30–3.15).

entities.name: PMID:31950372
observations: Nationwide Japan time-stratified case-crossover study using 30,435 AMI admissions from April 2012 to March 2016.
Asian dust two days before admission was associated with MINOCA (OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.18–2.29), but not MI with coronary artery disease; findings persisted in two-pollutant models.

entities.name: Asian dust
observations: Windblown mineral dust originating mainly from deserts in China and Mongolia; exposure is measured using observed Asian-dust events/visibility criteria in the cited Japanese studies.

entities.name: Acute myocardial infarction
observations: Short-term Asian/desert dust exposure was associated with AMI onset in the primary Western Japan study and in an independent Kumamoto study; later nationwide evidence supports an association particularly for MINOCA.
The evidence is observational and concerns short-term triggering/onset risk rather than proof that dust causes long-term baseline AMI incidence.
